paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by deficiency of tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2), a Janus kinase that mediates signaling by several cytokines. The first reported patient had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES). He had atopic dermatitis and elevated serum IgE, together with unusual susceptibility to viruses, fungi, and mycobacteria (Minegishi et al., 2006). Most patients reported later had mycobacterial and/or viral infections without features of HIES. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infection, caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta, and that HIES does not appear to be an intrinsic feature of the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, the third child of healthy first-cousin parents, who was vaccinated with BCG at 2 months of age. He developed left axillary lymphadenopathy at 8 months and generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue at 21 months. On admission he had fever and fistulous, enlarged, bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining cervical sinuses. His condition improved with antimycobacterial treatment, without relapse. At 8 years of age he had fever, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness, and blood and CSF cultures were positive for Brucella. After treatment he had hearing loss (92 dB in the right ear and 82 dB in the left), severe cognitive impairment, and pneumonia, and MRI showed lacunar infarcts in the left temporal and occipital lobes and in both parietal lobes. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the right maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with intravenous acyclovir. He had no skeletal or dental manifestations of HIES and no history of atopy, asthma, candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscess. His serum IgE was normal or only slightly high (highest value 218 IU/ml, at 16 years of age). At 2 years of age his serum IgG, IgM, and IgA, his lymphocyte subsets, and his nitroblue tetrazolium test were normal, but his antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low (0.69 IU/ml; normal, 2-20). Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the previously reported Japanese patient, their patient had none of the cardinal features of HIES.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) updated the clinical history of the original Japanese patient (P1), who was born to consanguineous parents. He had had atopic dermatitis since 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections since 1 year. He developed BCGitis at 22 months, 6 months after vaccination. He also had repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, pneumonia without pneumatocele formation, otitis, and sinusitis. At 15 years of age he had sepsis following severe nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis. Other infections included parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections associated with tonsillitis, molluscum contagiosum, and mild oral candidiasis. He repeatedly had hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and serum IgE concentrations of 1,430 to 2,100 IU/ml, and his NIH HIES score was 48 points. At 30 years of age he had ocular sarcoidosis.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) described 7 further TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. All had received BCG vaccine. None had atopy, high serum IgE, staphylococcal disease, other documented pyogenic infections, or fungal infections, including mucocutaneous candidiasis. P2 was the Turkish patient reported by Kilic et al. (2012). P3 and P4 were Moroccan sibs born to first-cousin parents. P3, a girl, was hospitalized at 13 years with abdominal tuberculosis and developed ascites, a psoas abscess from which M. tuberculosis was isolated, and disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis; she died after bacterial meningitis, 15 months after onset. Her brother, P4, was hospitalized at 8 months with meningitis of unknown etiology, and had recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels. P5 and P6 were Iranian sibs born to consanguineous parents. P5, a boy, developed right axillary and multiple cervical lymphadenitis at 2 and 4 months of age, and paravertebral and psoas abscesses with fistulization and pulmonary involvement at 4.5 years. He was treated with antimycobacterial drugs, surgery, and IFN-gamma. His sister, P6, developed BCG lymphadenopathy after vaccination and was hospitalized at 1 year for an unknown viral skin infection. P7, a 9-year-old Iranian girl born to consanguineous parents, had miliary tuberculosis with diffuse bilateral micronodular lung infiltrates, hilar and mediastinal adenopathy, and cavitary consolidation; M. tuberculosis was identified in gastric washes. P8, an 11-year-old adopted Argentinian boy, had herpes gingivostomatitis at 18 months and at almost 6 years, aseptic meningitis and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions at 24 months, and aseptic herpes meningitis with disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions at 10 years. He also had mild mental disability of uncertain origin and was maintained on acyclovir prophylaxis. Kreins et al. (2015) noted that P4 and P5 had a pure MSMD phenotype and P3 and P7 a pure tuberculosis phenotype, whereas P2, P6, and P8 resembled patients with partial autosomal recessive STAT1 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy born to young nonconsanguineous parents. After BCG vaccination on day 3 of life, he had repeated abscess formation and ulceration at the injection site, which healed by 10 months of age. At 14 months he developed BCG-associated tuberculosis of a left axillary lymph node; acid-fast bacilli were seen and M. bovis BCG was isolated, and there was no lung involvement. From 6 months of age he had recurrent respiratory tract infections (pneumonia or upper respiratory tract infection every 1 to 2 months) and diarrhea. Pathogens identified included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and BCG, and IgM serology was positive for influenza A and B viruses. He had no high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal disease, or lymphopenia. He had a small head circumference and spoke his first simple words at 3 years 4 months, with normal motor development. At 1 year 11 months his serum immunoglobulins, including IgE (27.4 IU/ml), were normal. The percentage of CD19+ B cells was increased (26.6%) and the percentage of CD3-CD16/CD56+ NK cells was decreased (3.6%). In a review of 12 reported TYK2-deficient patients, including their own, Wu et al. (2020) found that 7 (58%) had intracellular bacterial infections and 7 (58%) had recurrent viral infections, 3 (25%) had markedly increased serum IgE, and 2 (17%) had rash or atopic dermatitis/eczema. None had the special facial features, abnormal bone development or pathologic fractures, delayed loss of deciduous teeth, or aneurysms of STAT3-related hyper-IgE syndrome.
